turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Miss Bennet, that you should take the word of a young man like Mr. Wickham over mine, particularly when I have had every opportunity to prove my good character.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find it most distressing that you should so readily believe the malicious slanders of a man like Wickham, who has had the audacity to besmirch my good name.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Miss Bennet, it is your own prejudices and preconceptions that have led you to judge me so harshly, rather than any true understanding of my character or actions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your words, Mr. Darcy. You have consistently shown yourself to be proud, haughty, and dismissive of those you deem inferior. I have every reason to distrust you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You have shown no signs of change, Mr. Darcy, no indication that you are capable of humility or empathy. Your words are empty, and I will not be swayed by them.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be won over by your declarations of love, Mr. Darcy, when you have shown me time and again that you value your own pride and status above all else.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am astonished that you should think I would believe your declarations of love, Mr. Darcy, when you have shown such disregard for my feelings and my family's well-being in the past.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be so foolish as to think that a few well-timed words can erase the harm you have caused, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How dare you try to convince me that your sudden interest in me is genuine, when I have seen the way you have treated those around you with disdain and superiority?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Elizabeth, that you should refuse my proposal, given the sincerity of my words and the respect I have always shown you. Your behavior towards me, on the other hand, has been marked by ingratitude and a lack of understanding. I must confess, I find your refusal to be a considerable blow to my pride.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find your refusal to be a considerable blow to my pride, and I am at a loss to understand why you continue to harbor such ill will towards me, when I have done everything in my power to make amends for past slights.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you reconsider your refusal, Elizabeth. Your rejection wounds me deeply, and I fear it will be a long time before I can forgive the slight to my honor.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must admit, I am beginning to question the soundness of my judgment in pursuing a relationship with one who so callously disregards the feelings of others, including my own.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your obstinacy is as tiresome as it is astonishing, Elizabeth. I fail to comprehend why you refuse to see the sincerity of my intentions and the advantages that a union between us would bring.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that your words have stung me more than I would have believed possible. Your refusal to consider my proposal has left me feeling...disappointed, to say the least.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Elizabeth, that your behavior is a perfect example of the very prejudices and misconceptions that I have long sought to overcome in my interactions with you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Elizabeth, your refusal is a testament to your own limitations, rather than any fault of mine.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Elizabeth, that your rejection of my proposal is a disappointment, not to me, but to your own family, who have long hoped for a union between us.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your family's hopes and expectations are of no consequence to me, Elizabeth. It is your own happiness, or lack thereof, that I have been endeavoring to secure.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find it quite astonishing that you would so callously dismiss the sentiments I have expressed, and the sacrifices I have made, on your behalf.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
